$$
u={x}^{4}+11.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u={x}^{3}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}{({x}^{4}+11)}^{9}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{4}+11)^{9}\cdot {x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{9}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{9}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{9}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{10}}{10}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{40}{u}^{10}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{40}({x}^{4}+11)^{10}+C.\end{aligned}

In this case, the $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}-35).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.
So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}-35.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x({x}^{2}-35)^{10}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-35)^{10}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{10}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{10}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{10}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{11}}{11}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{22}{u}^{11}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{22}({x}^{2}-35)^{11}+C \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-35)^{11}}{22}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}+10).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.
So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}+10.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x({x}^{2}+10)^{10}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}+10)^{10}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{10}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{10}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{10}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{11}}{11}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{22}{u}^{11}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{22}({x}^{2}+10)^{11}+C \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+10)^{11}}{22}+C.\end{aligned}

In this case, the term $2{x}^{5}$ outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of ${x}^{6}-34.$ But the derivative is $6{x}^{5},$ so we're only out by a constant factor.
So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{6}-34.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{5}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u=2{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{5}({x}^{6}-34)^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{6}-34)^{5}\cdot 2{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{18}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{18}({x}^{6}-34)^{6}+C \\  & =\frac{({x}^{6}-34)^{6}}{18}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
u={x}^{7}-29.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =7{x}^{6}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{7}\text{d}u={x}^{6}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{6}({x}^{7}-29)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{7}-29)^{2}\cdot {x}^{6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{7}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\int {u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{7}\int {u}^{2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{21}{u}^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{21}({x}^{7}-29)^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{({x}^{7}-29)^{3}}{21}+C.\end{aligned}

knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the term ${x}^{6}$ outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of ${x}^{7}+15.$ But the derivative is $7{x}^{6},$ so we're only out by a constant factor.
So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{7}+15.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =7{x}^{6}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{7}\text{d}u={x}^{6}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{6}({x}^{7}+15)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{7}+15)^{2}\cdot {x}^{6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{7}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\int {u}^{2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{7}\int {u}^{2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3}}{3}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{21}{u}^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{21}({x}^{7}+15)^{3}+C \\  & =\frac{({x}^{7}+15)^{3}}{21}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}

$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}{(-25-{x}^{2})}^{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{{(-25-{x}^{2})}^{6}}{12}+C.\end{aligned}

In this case, the $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(-11-{x}^{2}).$ But the derivative is $-2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u=-11-{x}^{2}.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =-2x\,⟹\,(-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{(-11-{x}^{2})}^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int {(-11-{x}^{2})}^{5}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{12}{(-11-{x}^{2})}^{6}+C \\  & =-\frac{{(-11-{x}^{2})}^{6}}{12}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}-19).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.
So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}-19.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x({x}^{2}-19)^{3}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-19)^{3}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{3}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{3}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{u}^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}-19)^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-19)^{4}}{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}+26).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.
So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}+26.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x({x}^{2}+26)^{3}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}+26)^{3}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{3}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{3}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{4}}{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{u}^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{8}({x}^{2}+26)^{4}+C \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}+26)^{4}}{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the ${x}^{2}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(2{x}^{3}-26).$ But the derivative is $6{x}^{2},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u=2{x}^{3}-26.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{(2{x}^{3}-26)}^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}-26)^{5}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}(2{x}^{3}-26)^{6}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

So we make the substitution

$$
u=2{x}^{3}+4.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{(2{x}^{3}+4)}^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}+4)^{5}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}(2{x}^{3}+4)^{6}+C.\end{aligned}

knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the ${x}^{2}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $(2{x}^{3}+33).$ But the derivative is $6{x}^{2},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u=2{x}^{3}+33.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =6{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{(2{x}^{3}+33)}^{5}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2{x}^{3}+33)^{5}\cdot {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {u}^{5}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}\int {u}^{5}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{{u}^{6}}{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}{u}^{6}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{36}(2{x}^{3}+33)^{6}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $2{x}^{7}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{8}-19).$ But the derivative is $8{x}^{7},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{8}-19.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =8{x}^{7}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u={x}^{7}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{7}{({x}^{8}-19)}^{7}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{({x}^{8}-19)}^{7}\cdot {x}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2{u}^{7}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{8}}{8}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{u}^{8}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{({x}^{8}-19)}^{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $2{x}^{7}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{8}+11).$ But the derivative is $8{x}^{7},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{8}+11.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =8{x}^{7}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u={x}^{7}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{7}{({x}^{8}+11)}^{7}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{({x}^{8}+11)}^{7}\cdot {x}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2{u}^{7}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{8}}{8}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{u}^{8}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{({x}^{8}+11)}^{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $2{x}^{7}$ that's outside the parentheses isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{8}+40).$ But the derivative is $8{x}^{7},$ so we're only out by a constant factor. 

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{8}+40.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =8{x}^{7}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{8}\text{d}u={x}^{7}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{7}{({x}^{8}+40)}^{7}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{({x}^{8}+40)}^{7}\cdot {x}^{7}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 2{u}^{7}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{7}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{u}^{8}}{8}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{u}^{8}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{32}{({x}^{8}+40)}^{8}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the $x$ that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}-40).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}-40.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-40}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{{x}^{2}-40}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{({x}^{2}-40)^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of $(26-{x}^{2}).$ But the derivative is $- 2 x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u=26-{x}^{2}.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =- 2 x\,⟹\,(- \frac{1}{2})\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{26-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{26-{x}^{2}}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\ & =\int \sqrt{u}\cdot (- \frac{1}{2})\text{d}u \\ & =- \frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}- \frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =(- \frac{1}{2})\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\ & =(- \frac{1}{2})\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2}+C \\ & =- \frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\ & =- \frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\ & =- \frac{1}{3}\sqrt{(26-{x}^{2})^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
